claim: Cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that mediates many oxidation/reduction reactions of proteins.
source: Cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that mediates many oxidation/reduction reactions of proteins, is the redox center of the abundant antioxidant tripeptide glutathione which also serves as a major cysteine reserve, and is essential for iron-sulfur cluster assembly in the mitochondrion (Wu et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2004 and Zheng et al., 1993

claim: Cysteine is the redox center of the abundant antioxidant tripeptide glutathione which also serves as a major cysteine reserve.
source: Cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that mediates many oxidation/reduction reactions of proteins, is the redox center of the abundant antioxidant tripeptide glutathione which also serves as a major cysteine reserve, and is essential for iron-sulfur cluster assembly in the mitochondrion (Wu et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2004 and Zheng et al., 1993

claim: Cysteine is essential for iron-sulfur cluster assembly in the mitochondrion.
source: Cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that mediates many oxidation/reduction reactions of proteins, is the redox center of the abundant antioxidant tripeptide glutathione which also serves as a major cysteine reserve, and is essential for iron-sulfur cluster assembly in the mitochondrion (Wu et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2004 and Zheng et al., 1993

claim: Cysteine residues in many proteins are oxidized in the endoplasmic reticulum to form intra- and interprotein disulfide linkages, most commonly in secreted proteins.
source: Cysteine residues in many proteins are in close proximity in the primary or folded protein sequence and are oxidized in the endoplasmic reticulum to form intra- and interprotein disulfide linkages, most commonly in secreted proteins which mediate intercellular signaling and defense (Noiva, 1994; Raina and Missiakas, 1997; Rietsch and Beckwith, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Noiva, 1994; Raina and Missiakas, 1997; Rietsch and Beckwith, 1998

claim: The reactivity of the cysteine sulfur is key for the coordination of metals such as zinc or iron in many enzymes.
source: In many enzymes, the reactivity of the cysteine sulfur is key for the coordination of metals such as zinc or iron, which support protein structure and catalytic activity (Giles et al., 2003; Tainer et al., 1991; Miller et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to Giles et al., 2003; Tainer et al., 1991; Miller et al., 1985

claim: Cysteine is a key source of hydrogen sulfide (H2S), a volatile signaling molecule.
source: Cysteine is also a key source of hydrogen sulfide (H2S), a volatile signaling molecule (Singh and Banerjee, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singh and Banerjee, 2011

claim: High levels of cysteine impair mitochondrial respiration by disrupting iron homeostasis.
source: High levels of cysteine impair mitochondrial respiration by disrupting iron homeostasis (Hughes et al., 2020), acts as a neural excitotoxin (Olney et al., 1990), and promotes the formation of toxic levels of hydrogen sulfide gas (Singh and Banerjee, 2011; Evans, 1967; Truong et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2020

claim: Excess cysteine acts as a neural excitotoxin.
source: High levels of cysteine impair mitochondrial respiration by disrupting iron homeostasis (Hughes et al., 2020), acts as a neural excitotoxin (Olney et al., 1990), and promotes the formation of toxic levels of hydrogen sulfide gas (Singh and Banerjee, 2011; Evans, 1967; Truong et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olney et al., 1990

claim: Excess cysteine promotes the formation of toxic levels of hydrogen sulfide gas.
source: High levels of cysteine impair mitochondrial respiration by disrupting iron homeostasis (Hughes et al., 2020), acts as a neural excitotoxin (Olney et al., 1990), and promotes the formation of toxic levels of hydrogen sulfide gas (Singh and Banerjee, 2011; Evans, 1967; Truong et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Singh and Banerjee, 2011; Evans, 1967; Truong et al., 2006

claim: CDO1-mediated oxidation is the primary pathway of cysteine catabolism when sulfur amino acid availability is normal or high.
source: CDO1-mediated oxidation is the primary pathway of cysteine catabolism when sulfur amino acid (methionine or cysteine) availability is normal or high (Bella et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bella et al., 1996

claim: Cystathionine is catabolized by cystathionase (CTH-2 in C. elegans, CTH in mammals) producing cysteine and α-ketobutyrate.
source: Cystathionine is catabolized by cystathionase (CTH-2 in Caenorhabditis elegans, CTH in mammals) producing cysteine and α-ketobutyrate.
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript describing the metabolic pathway

claim: Cysteine is oxidized to cysteinesulfinate by cysteine dioxygenase (CDO-1 in C. elegans, CDO1 in mammals) using dissolved atmospheric dioxygen.
source: Cysteine is further oxidized using dissolved atmospheric dioxygen to cysteinesulfinate by cysteine dioxygenase (CDO-1 in C. elegans, CDO1 in mammals; Figure 1A; Stipanuk, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stipanuk, 2004 and shown in Figure 1A

claim: The oxidation of cysteinesulfinate downstream of CDO-1 generates highly toxic sulfites that are normally oxidized to more benign sulfate by sulfite oxidase.
source: The further oxidation of cysteinesulfinate downstream of CDO-1 generates highly toxic sulfites that are normally oxidized to more benign sulfate by sulfite oxidase (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A metabolic pathway diagram

claim: The activity and abundance of CDO1 increase dramatically in cells and animals fed excess cysteine and methionine.
source: As a critical player in cysteine homeostasis, CDO1 is a highly regulated enzyme: the activity and abundance of CDO1 increase dramatically in cells and animals fed excess cysteine and methionine (Stipanuk and Ueki, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stipanuk and Ueki, 2011

claim: CDO1 levels are governed both transcriptionally and post-translationally via proteasomal degradation.
source: CDO1 levels are governed both transcriptionally and post-translationally via proteasomal degradation (Dominy et al., 2006a; Dominy et al., 2006b; Stipanuk et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2004; Kwon and Stipanuk, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: CDO1 is a tumor suppressor whose activity is silenced in diverse cancers via promoter methylation.
source: CDO1 is a tumor suppressor whose activity is silenced in diverse cancers via promoter methylation, a potential biomarker of tumor grade and progression (Kojima et al., 2018; Yamashita et al., 2018; Brait et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kojima et al., 2018; Yamashita et al., 2018; Brait et al., 2012

claim: Decreased CDO1 activity may support tumor cell growth by reducing reactive oxygen species and decreasing drug susceptibility.
source: Decreased CDO1 activity may support tumor cell growth by reducing reactive oxygen species and decreasing drug susceptibility (Kang et al., 2019; Jeschke et al., 2013; Hao et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kang et al., 2019; Jeschke et al., 2013; Hao et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2022

claim: CDO-1 is a key player in the pathophysiology of isolated sulfite oxidase deficiency (ISOD) and molybdenum cofactor deficiency (MoCD).
source: Using the nematode C. elegans, we have previously shown that CDO-1 is a key player in the pathophysiology of two fatal inborn errors of metabolism; isolated sulfite oxidase deficiency (ISOD) and molybdenum cofactor deficiency (MoCD; Duran et al., 1978; Mudd et al., 1967).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duran et al., 1978; Mudd et al., 1967 and prior work by the authors

claim: Molybdenum cofactor (Moco) is an essential 520 Dalton prosthetic group synthesized from GTP by a conserved multistep biosynthetic pathway.
source: Molybdenum cofactor (Moco) is an essential 520 Dalton prosthetic group synthesized from GTP by a conserved multistep biosynthetic pathway that is present in about 2/3 of bacterial genomes and nearly all eukaryotic genomes (Schwarz et al., 2009; Zhang and Gladyshev, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwarz et al., 2009; Zhang and Gladyshev, 2008

claim: C. elegans can either retrieve Moco synthesized by the bacteria it consumes or can synthesize Moco de novo using its own Moco biosynthetic pathway.
source: C. elegans can either retrieve Moco synthesized by the bacteria it consumes or can synthesize Moco de novo using its own Moco biosynthetic pathway (Warnhoff and Ruvkun, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warnhoff and Ruvkun, 2019

claim: C. elegans strains carrying mutations in genes encoding Moco biosynthetic enzymes (moc) feeding on wild-type E. coli develop normally.
source: C. elegans strains carrying mutations in genes encoding Moco biosynthetic enzymes (moc) and feeding on wild-type E. coli develop normally.
evidence: Stated as an observation from prior work

claim: moc-mutant C. elegans when fed on Moco-deficient E. coli are inviable, arresting development at an early larval stage.
source: Yet, these same moc-mutant C. elegans when fed on Moco-deficient E. coli as their sole nutritional source are inviable, arresting development at an early larval stage.
evidence: Stated as an observation from prior work

claim: A saturated genetic selection for mutations that suppress Moco-deficient inviability identified multiple independent mutations in cth-2 or cdo-1.
source: A saturated genetic selection for mutations that suppress this inviability identified multiple independent mutations in cth-2 or cdo-1, genes which encode enzymes in the cysteine biosynthetic and degradation pathway.
evidence: Stated as a result from prior genetic screen

claim: The toxic sulfites produced downstream of CDO-1 are normally oxidized to more benign sulfate by Moco-requiring sulfite oxidase (SUOX-1 in C. elegans, SUOX in mammals).
source: The toxic sulfites produced downstream of CDO-1 are normally oxidized to more benign sulfate by Moco-requiring sulfite oxidase (SUOX-1 in C. elegans, SUOX in mammals) an essential enzyme in C. elegans and humans (Figure 1A; Mudd et al., 1967; Warnhoff and Ruvkun, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mudd et al., 1967; Warnhoff and Ruvkun, 2019 and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Loss of cdo-1 or cth-2 suppresses the lethality caused by both Moco and sulfite oxidase deficiencies in C. elegans by preventing the production of toxic sulfites.
source: Therefore, loss of cdo-1 or cth-2 suppresses the lethality caused by both Moco and sulfite oxidase deficiencies in C. elegans by preventing the production of toxic sulfites (Warnhoff and Ruvkun, 2019; Warnhoff et al., 2021; Snoozy et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Warnhoff and Ruvkun, 2019; Warnhoff et al., 2021; Snoozy et al., 2022

claim: An unbiased genetic screen identified multiple independent loss-of-function mutations in egl-9 and rhy-1 that dramatically increase expression of a Pcdo-1::CDO-1::GFP transgene.
source: We identified multiple independent loss-of-function mutations in two genes, egl-9 and rhy-1, that dramatically increase expression of this Pcdo-1::CDO-1::GFP transgene.
evidence: Described as a result from the genetic screen performed in this study

claim: egl-9 encodes the O2-sensing prolyl hydroxylase and orthologue of mammalian EglN1.
source: egl-9 encodes the O2 -sensing prolyl hydroxylase and orthologue of mammalian EglN1.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about egl-9

claim: rhy-1 encodes the regulator of hypoxia inducible transcription factor, an enzyme with homology to membrane-bound O-acyltransferases.
source: rhy-1 encodes the regulator of hypoxia inducible transcription factor, an enzyme with homology to membrane-bound O-acyltransferases (Shen et al., 2006; Epstein et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen et al., 2006; Epstein et al., 2001

claim: Inactivation of egl-9 or rhy-1 activates a transcriptional program mediated by the hypoxia inducible transcription factor, HIF-1.
source: Inactivation of egl-9 or rhy-1 activates a transcriptional program mediated by the hypoxia inducible transcription factor, HIF-1 (Shen et al., 2006; Epstein et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen et al., 2006; Epstein et al., 2001

claim: The egl-9(sa307) and rhy-1(ok1402) mutations dramatically induce expression of GFP driven by the Pcdo-1::GFP transcriptional reporter transgene.
source: The egl-9(sa307) and rhy-1(ok1402) mutations dramatically induce expression of GFP driven by the Pcdo-1::GFP transcriptional reporter transgene (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1D and E with quantification

claim: egl-9 and rhy-1 are necessary for the normal transcriptional repression of cdo-1.
source: Furthermore, these data demonstrate that egl-9 and rhy-1 are necessary for the normal transcriptional repression of cdo-1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of egl-9 or rhy-1 increases cdo-1 transcription

claim: The Pcdo-1::CDO-1::GFP fusion protein is functional and rescues a cdo-1 loss-of-function mutation.
source: The Pcdo-1::CDO-1::GFP fusion protein was functional and rescued a cdo-1 loss-of-function mutation: the Pcdo-1::CDO-1::GFP fusion protein reverses the suppression of Moco-deficient lethality caused by cdo-1 loss of function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: A transgene expressing an active-site mutant Pcdo-1::CDO-1[C85Y]::GFP does not rescue the cdo-1 mutant phenotype.
source: However, rescue experiments with a prolyl hydroxylase domain-inactive egl-9(H487A) transgene do not correct the accumulation of HIF-1 protein and only partially reduce the HIF-1 transcriptional output (Shao et al., 2009). Through our studies of cdo-1 transcription, we demonstrate that an egl-9(H487A) mutant incompletely activates HIF-1 transcription when compared to an egl-9(-) null mutation (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: rhy-1 and egl-9 act in a pathway that regulates the abundance and activity of the HIF-1 transcription factor.
source: rhy-1 and egl-9 act in a pathway that regulates the abundance and activity of the HIF-1 transcription factor (Shen et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2012

claim: The activity of rhy-1 is most upstream in the pathway and negatively regulates the activity of cysl-1.
source: The activity of rhy-1 is most upstream in the pathway and negatively regulates the activity of cysl-1, which encodes a cysteine synthase-like enzyme of probable algal origin (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2022

claim: CYSL-1 directly binds to and inhibits EGL-9 in an H2S-modulated manner.
source: CYSL-1 directly binds to and inhibits EGL-9 in an H2S-modulated manner (Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 2012

claim: EGL-9 uses molecular oxygen as well as an α-ketoglutarate cofactor to directly inhibit HIF-1 via prolyl hydroxylation.
source: EGL-9 uses molecular oxygen as well as an α-ketoglutarate cofactor to directly inhibit HIF-1 via prolyl hydroxylation, which recruits the VHL-1 ubiquitin ligase to ubiquitinate HIF-1, targeting it for degradation by the proteasome (Figure 5A) (Salceda and Caro, 1997; Huang et al., 1998; Sutter et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Salceda and Caro, 1997; Huang et al., 1998; Sutter et al., 2000 and shown in Figure 5A

claim: Prolyl hydroxylation of HIF-1 recruits the VHL-1 ubiquitin ligase to ubiquitinate HIF-1, targeting it for degradation by the proteasome.
source: EGL-9 uses molecular oxygen as well as an α-ketoglutarate cofactor to directly inhibit HIF-1 via prolyl hydroxylation, which recruits the VHL-1 ubiquitin ligase to ubiquitinate HIF-1, targeting it for degradation by the proteasome (Figure 5A) (Salceda and Caro, 1997; Huang et al., 1998; Sutter et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Salceda and Caro, 1997; Huang et al., 1998; Sutter et al., 2000 and shown in Figure 5A

claim: The induction of Pcdo-1::GFP by egl-9 inactivation was dependent upon the activity of hif-1, but not on the activity of cysl-1.
source: The induction of Pcdo-1::GFP by egl-9 inactivation was dependent upon the activity of hif-1, but not on the activity of cysl-1 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: Induction of Pcdo-1::GFP by rhy-1 inactivation was dependent upon the activity of both hif-1 and cysl-1.
source: In contrast, induction of Pcdo-1::GFP by rhy-1 inactivation was dependent upon the activity of both hif-1 and cysl-1 (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 2A and C

claim: rhy-1, cysl-1, and egl-9 function in a negative-regulatory cascade to control the activity of HIF-1 which transcriptionally activates cdo-1.
source: These results reveal a genetic pathway whereby rhy-1, cysl-1, and egl-9 function in a negative-regulatory cascade to control the activity of HIF-1 which transcriptionally activates cdo-1.
evidence: Inferred from the epistasis experiments shown in Figure 2

claim: egl-9(-) mutant C. elegans display an eightfold increase in cdo-1 mRNA compared to wild type.
source: egl-9(-) mutant C. elegans display an eightfold increase in cdo-1 mRNA compared to wild type.
evidence: Stated as a result from published RNA-seq data (Pender and Horvitz, 2018)

claim: The induction of cdo-1 mRNA by egl-9(-) mutation was completely suppressed by a hif-1(-) mutation.
source: This induction was dependent on hif-1; a hif-1(-) mutation completely suppressed the induction of cdo-1 mRNA caused by an egl-9(-) mutation (Pender and Horvitz, 2018).
evidence: Stated as a result from published RNA-seq data (Pender and Horvitz, 2018)

claim: HIF-1 directly binds the cdo-1 promoter.
source: ChIP-seq data of HIF-1 performed by the modERN project show that HIF-1 directly binds the cdo-1 promoter (peak from –1165 to –714 base pairs 5' to the cdo-1 ATG start codon; Kudron et al., 2018; Vora et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to ChIP-seq data from Kudron et al., 2018; Vora et al., 2022

claim: The HIF-1 binding site in the cdo-1 promoter contains three copies of the HIF-binding motif (5'-RCGTG-3').
source: This HIF-1 binding site contains three copies of the HIF-binding motif (5'-RCGTG-3'; Kaelin and Ratcliffe, 2008).
evidence: Stated as an observation with citation to Kaelin and Ratcliffe, 2008 for the motif

claim: cdo-1 is a downstream effector of HIF-1 and is likely a direct transcriptional target of HIF-1.
source: Thus, cdo-1 is a downstream effector of HIF-1 and is likely a direct transcriptional target of HIF-1.
evidence: Inferred from HIF-1 binding to cdo-1 promoter and genetic epistasis data

claim: Mammalian CDO1 levels and activity are highly induced by dietary cysteine.
source: Mammalian CDO1 levels and activity are highly induced by dietary cysteine (Bella et al., 1996; Stipanuk, 2004; Stipanuk and Ueki, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bella et al., 1996; Stipanuk, 2004; Stipanuk and Ueki, 2011

claim: High levels of cysteine promoted cdo-1 transcription in C. elegans.
source: Like our egl-9 and rhy-1 loss-of-function mutations, high levels of cysteine promoted cdo-1 transcription (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3A-C

claim: 100 μM supplemental cysteine caused a significant 3.6-fold induction of Pcdo-1::GFP.
source: Despite the significant 3.6-fold induction of Pcdo-1::GFP caused by 100 μM supplemental cysteine, we note that this induction is not as dramatic as the induction caused by null mutations in egl-9 or rhy-1.
evidence: Quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: cysl-1(-) and hif-1(-) mutant animals cannot survive in a high cysteine environment.
source: However, this experiment was not possible as we observed 100% lethality in cysl-1(-) and hif-1(-) mutant animals exposed to 100 μM supplemental cysteine, a cysteine concentration at which wild-type animals are healthy (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3E

claim: cysl-1 and hif-1 are necessary for survival under high cysteine conditions.
source: While this phenotype limits our ability to establish the role of cysl-1 and hif-1 in the induction of cdo-1 by high levels of cysteine, these data demonstrate that cysl-1 and hif-1 are necessary for survival under high cysteine conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the lethality of cysl-1(-) and hif-1(-) mutants in high cysteine

claim: egl-9(-) and rhy-1(-) mutant C. elegans were partially viable when exposed to 1000 μM supplemental cysteine, a concentration that causes 100% lethality in wild-type animals.
source: Indeed, we found that egl-9(-) and rhy-1(-) mutant C. elegans were partially viable when exposed to 1000 μM supplemental cysteine, a concentration that causes 100% lethality in wild-type animals (Figure 3F).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3F

claim: egl-9 and rhy-1 are negative regulators of cysteine tolerance.
source: Thus, egl-9 and rhy-1 are negative regulators cysteine tolerance.
evidence: Inferred from the increased cysteine resistance of egl-9(-) and rhy-1(-) mutants

claim: The RHY-1/CYSL-1/EGL-9/HIF-1 pathway plays a critical physiological role in promoting cysteine homeostasis.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate a critical physiological role for the RHY-1/CYSL-1/EGL-9/HIF-1 pathway in promoting cysteine homeostasis.
evidence: Inferred from the cysteine sensitivity and resistance phenotypes observed

claim: High levels of cysteine caused no difference in Pcdo-1::GFP expression in egl-9(-) mutant animals.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we saw no difference in Pcdo-1::GFP expression in egl-9(-) mutant animals exposed to 0 or 100 μM supplemental cysteine (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: High levels of cysteine caused a significant induction of Pcdo-1::GFP in the rhy-1(-) mutant background.
source: In contrast to our results with egl-9(-), we observed that high levels of cysteine caused a significant induction of Pcdo-1::GFP in the rhy-1(-) mutant background (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: Cysteine acts in a pathway with egl-9 but operates in parallel to the function of rhy-1.
source: These data suggest that cysteine acts in a pathway with egl-9 but operates in parallel to the function of rhy-1.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of cysteine on Pcdo-1::GFP in egl-9(-) vs rhy-1(-) backgrounds

claim: cdo-1(-) mutant animals were not sensitive to high levels of supplemental cysteine compared to the wild type.
source: cdo-1(-) mutant animals were not sensitive to high levels of supplemental cysteine compared to the wild type (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 3D-F

claim: cdo-1 is not necessary for survival under high cysteine conditions.
source: Thus, cdo-1 is not necessary for survival under high cysteine conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of cysteine sensitivity in cdo-1(-) mutants

claim: Alternate pathways exist that promote cysteine homeostasis beyond cdo-1.
source: This suggests the existence of alternate pathways that promote cysteine homeostasis.
evidence: Inferred from cdo-1(-) mutants surviving high cysteine despite cdo-1's role in cysteine catabolism

claim: HIF-1 activates pathways (in addition to cdo-1) that promote survival under high cysteine conditions.
source: Given the role of the RHY-1/CYSL-1/EGL-9/HIF-1 pathway in promoting cysteine homeostasis, we propose that HIF-1 activates pathways (in addition to cdo-1) that promote survival under high cysteine conditions.
evidence: Proposed based on the requirement of hif-1 for cysteine survival but not cdo-1

claim: The cdo-1(rae273) allele encodes a C-terminal tagged 'CDO-1::GFP' fusion protein from the native cdo-1 genomic locus.
source: This cdo-1(rae273) allele encodes a C-terminal tagged 'CDO-1::GFP' fusion protein from the native cdo-1 genomic locus (Figure 4A).
evidence: Described as a CRISPR/Cas9-generated allele and shown in Figure 4A

claim: The CDO-1::GFP fusion protein encoded by cdo-1(rae273) is functional.
source: The moc-1(-) mutant C. elegans expressing CDO-1::GFP from the native cdo-1 locus arrest during larval development when fed Moco-deficient E. coli, but not when fed Moco-producing E. coli (Figure 4C). This lethality is caused by the CDO-1-mediated production of sulfites which are only toxic when C. elegans is Moco deficient, and demonstrates that the CDO-1::GFP fusion protein is functional (Warnhoff and Ruvkun, 2019).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 4C

claim: CDO-1::GFP is expressed in multiple tissues, including prominent expression in the hypodermis.
source: When wild-type animals expressing CDO-1::GFP were grown under standard culture conditions, we observed CDO-1::GFP expression in multiple tissues, including prominent expression in the hypodermis (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed by microscopy and shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: CDO-1::GFP fusion protein levels, encoded by cdo-1(rae273), were increased by egl-9(-) or rhy-1(-) mutations.
source: We found that CDO-1::GFP fusion protein levels, encoded by cdo-1(rae273), were increased by egl-9(-) or rhy-1(-) mutations (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: High levels of cysteine promoted accumulation of CDO-1::GFP.
source: Furthermore, high levels of cysteine also promoted accumulation of CDO-1::GFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The hypodermis was the most prominent site of CDO-1::GFP accumulation.
source: In all scenarios, the hypodermis was the most prominent site of CDO-1::GFP accumulation.
evidence: Observed across multiple experimental conditions

claim: CDO-1::GFP was expressed in the cytoplasm of Hyp7, the major C. elegans hypodermal cell.
source: Specifically, we found that CDO-1::GFP was expressed in the cytoplasm of Hyp7, the major C. elegans hypodermal cell (Figure 4B).
evidence: Observed by microscopy and shown in Figure 4B

claim: Hypodermal-specific expression of cdo-1 is sufficient to rescue the cdo-1(-) mutant suppression of Moco-deficient larval arrest.
source: We found that multiple independent transgenic strains of cdo-1(-) moc-1(-) double mutant animals carrying the Pcol-10::CDO-1::GFP transgene displayed a larval arrest phenotype when fed a Moco-deficient diet (Figure 4D). These data demonstrated that hypodermal-specific expression of cdo-1 is sufficient to rescue the cdo-1(-) mutant suppression of Moco-deficient lethality.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 4D

claim: The rescue of cdo-1(-) mutant suppression by hypodermal cdo-1 expression was dependent upon the enzymatic activity of CDO-1.
source: This rescue was dependent upon the enzymatic activity of CDO-1 as an active site variant of this transgene (Pcol-10::CDO-1[C85Y]::GFP) did not rescue the suppressed larval arrest of cdo-1(-) moc-1(-) double mutant animals fed Moco-deficient diets (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 4D

claim: The hypodermis is a critical tissue for sulfur amino acid metabolism.
source: Our tissue-specific rescue data demonstrate that hypodermal expression of cdo-1 is sufficient to promote cysteine catabolism and suggest that the hypodermis is a critical tissue for sulfur amino acid metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from the tissue-specific rescue experiments

claim: Null mutations in suox-1 cause larval lethality.
source: Null mutations in suox-1 cause larval lethality.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: Animals carrying the suox-1(gk738847) hypomorphic allele are healthy under standard culture conditions.
source: However, animals carrying the suox-1(gk738847) hypomorphic allele are healthy under standard culture conditions (Warnhoff and Ruvkun, 2019; Warnhoff et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Warnhoff and Ruvkun, 2019; Warnhoff et al., 2021

claim: suox-1(gk738847) mutant animals display only 4% SUOX-1 activity compared to wild type and are exquisitely sensitive to sulfite stress.
source: suox-1(gk738847) mutant animals display only 4% SUOX-1 activity compared to wild type and are exquisitely sensitive to sulfite stress (Oliphant et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oliphant et al., 2023

claim: While egl-9(-) and suox-1(gk738847) single mutant animals are healthy under standard culture conditions, the egl-9(-); suox-1(gk738847) double mutant animals are extremely sick.
source: While egl-9(-) and suox-1(gk738847) single mutant animals are healthy under standard culture conditions, the egl-9(-); suox-1(gk738847) double mutant animals are extremely sick and require significantly more days to exhaust their E. coli food source under standard culture conditions (Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Table 1

claim: The egl-9; suox-1 synthetic sickness phenotype was suppressed by inactivating mutations in cdo-1 or cth-2.
source: The egl-9; suox-1 synthetic sickness phenotype was suppressed by inactivating mutations in cdo-1 or cth-2 which block the endogenous production of sulfite (Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Table 1

claim: The deleterious activity of the egl-9(-) mutation in a suox-1(gk738847) background requires functional sulfur amino acid metabolism.
source: These data demonstrate that the deleterious activity of the egl-9(-) mutation in a suox-1(gk738847) background requires functional sulfur amino acid metabolism.
evidence: Inferred from the suppression of the synthetic sickness by cdo-1 or cth-2 mutations

claim: The egl-9; suox-1 synthetic sickness phenotype was dependent upon hif-1 but not cysl-1.
source: The egl-9; suox-1 synthetic sickness phenotype was dependent upon hif-1 but not cysl-1 (Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally and shown in Table 1

claim: Transcriptional activation of cdo-1 by HIF-1 causes increased CDO-1 activity and increased flux of sulfur amino acids through their catabolic pathway.
source: These results are consistent with our proposed genetic pathway and support the model that transcriptional activation of cdo-1 by HIF-1 causes increased CDO-1 activity and increased flux of sulfur amino acids through their catabolic pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic epistasis experiments with suox-1
